newsitem.title: UK: Police accused in English miscarriage of justice.
newsitem.headline: Police accused in English miscarriage of justice.

text.p: A lawyer in England's latest miscarriage of justice case on Monday accused police of using oppression and deception to trick a defendant into confessing to the 1979 murder of schoolboy Carl Bridgewater.

Michael Hickey, his cousin Vincent Hickey and James Robinson -- known as the Bridgewater Three -- spent 18 years in prison before they were released in February after their conviction for the murder of the 13-year-old newspaper delivery boy was deemed unsafe.
They are now appealing against the original conviction in an attempt to clear their names.

Lawyer Michael Mansfield told an Appeal Court he would present new evidence to show that police had tricked a fourth defendant, Patrick Molloy, into signing a false confession on which the convictions are based. Molloy died in prison in 1981.
"That evidence, the turning point of the whole case was achieved by...oppression by police officers and by a carefully cultivated strategy of deception," he told the packed courtroom.
"This contrivance may be laid at the door of a particular squad of officers," he added.

The case is the latest in a series of judicial reversals in England. The "Guildford Four" and "Birmingham Six" were released following lengthy prison terms after being wrongly convicted of Irish Republican Army bombing on pubs that killed 26 people.
Mansfield said Molloy had been tricked into signing the admission after police told him Vincent Hickey had admitted to the crime, but police had concocted and forged the confession.
"There was no statement signed by Vincent Hickey," he said.
Mansfield said Malloy was questioned up to 30 times by police. The times of the interviews were not recorded and crucial notes went missing. There were also questions about how the notes were taken.
"The pattern of errors is enormous," Mansfield said.
Turning his attention to Molloy's confession, he said experts who examined the document doubted its authenticity and noted that the speed with which it was reportedly taken was also questionable.
He accused several police officers of wrongdoing and said one detective, who died in 1992, had been convicted by a police tribunal in 1989 for making a false witness statement about an interview.
A panel of three judges will rule on the appeal after the hearing which is expected to last four weeks.
